facts.statement: The dodo was first recorded by Dutch sailors in 1598.
facts.quote: The first recorded mention of the dodo was by Dutch sailors in 1598.

facts.statement: The last widely accepted sighting of the dodo occurred in 1662.
facts.quote: The last widely accepted sighting of a dodo was in 1662.

facts.statement: Subfossil remains indicate the dodo stood about 62.6 to 75 cm tall and weighed between 10.6 and 17.5 kg.
facts.quote: Subfossil remains show the dodo measured about 62.6 - 75 cm in height and may have weighed 10.6 - 17.5 kg in the wild.

facts.statement: The dodo used gizzard stones to digest food thought to include fruits and lived in the woods of drier coastal areas of Mauritius.
facts.quote: It used gizzard stones to help digest its food, which is thought to have included fruits, and its main habitat is believed to have been the woods in the drier coastal areas of Mauritius.

facts.statement: One account states that the dodo's clutch consisted of a single egg.
facts.quote: One account states its clutch consisted of a single egg.

facts.statement: The dodo and the Rodrigues solitaire formed the subtribe Raphina, which belongs to the family Columbidae.
facts.quote: The two formed the subtribe Raphina, a clade of extinct flightless birds that are a part of the group that includes pigeons and doves (the family Columbidae).

facts.statement: A dried head is the only remaining soft tissue of the dodo.
facts.quote: Among these is a dried head, the only soft tissue of the dodo that remains today.

facts.statement: Osteological and DNA analysis led to the dissolution of the family Raphidae, placing the dodo in the subfamily Raphinae and tribe Raphini.
facts.quote: Osteological and DNA analysis has since led to the dissolution of the family Raphidae, and the dodo and solitaire are now placed in the columbid subfamily Raphinae and tribe Raphini, along with their closest relatives.

facts.statement: The dodo's exact appearance in life and its behavior remain unresolved due to varying portraits and limited evidence from live specimens.
facts.quote: Since these portraits vary considerably, and since only some of the illustrations are known to have been drawn from live specimens, the dodos' exact appearance in life remains unresolved, and little is known about its behaviour.

facts.statement: It is now believed that the existence of a white dodo on Réunion was a confusion with the Réunion ibis and paintings.
facts.quote: A white dodo was once thought to have existed on the nearby island of Réunion, but it is now believed that this assumption was merely confusion based on the also-extinct Réunion ibis and paintings of white dodos.

facts.statement: Genetic analysis placed the dodo within the pigeon family Columbidae.
facts.quote: Comparison of mitochondrial cytochrome b and 12S rRNA sequences isolated from a tarsal of the Oxford specimen and a femur of a Rodrigues solitaire confirmed their close relationship and their placement within the Columbidae.

facts.statement: The Nicobar pigeon is considered the closest living relative of the dodo based on genetic evidence.
facts.quote: The genetic evidence was interpreted as showing the Southeast Asian Nicobar pigeon (Caloenas nicobarica) to be their closest living relative

facts.statement: Jolyon C. Parish proposed placing the dodo in the subfamily Gourinae based on behavioral and morphological evidence.
facts.quote: Jolyon C. Parish proposed that the dodo and Rodrigues solitaire should be placed in the subfamily Gourinae along with the Goura pigeons and others

facts.statement: Mathurin Jacques Brisson coined the genus name Raphus in 1760, establishing the current scientific name Raphus cucullatus.
facts.quote: Mathurin Jacques Brisson coined the genus name Raphus (referring to the bustards) in 1760, resulting in the current name Raphus cucullatus.

facts.statement: Carl Linnaeus coined the binomial name Didus ineptus in 1766, which is now a synonym of Raphus cucullatus.
facts.quote: In 1766, Linnaeus coined the new binomial Didus ineptus (meaning "inept dodo").

facts.statement: Genetic studies suggest the ancestors of the dodo diverged from other lineages approximately 23.03 million years ago.
facts.quote: The 2002 study indicated that the ancestors of the dodo and the solitaire diverged around the Paleogene-Neogene boundary, about 23.03 million years ago.

facts.statement: The Mascarene Islands, where the dodo lived, are volcanic islands less than 10 million years old.
facts.quote: The Mascarene Islands (Mauritius, Réunion, and Rodrigues), are of volcanic origin and are less than 10 million years old.

facts.statement: The absence of competing mammalian herbivores on the Mascarene Islands allowed the dodo to evolve large size and flightlessness.
facts.quote: The lack of mammalian herbivores competing for resources on these islands allowed the solitaire and the dodo to attain very large sizes and flightlessness.

facts.statement: Most historical representations depict the dodo with greyish or brownish plumage and a tuft of curly feathers on its rear.
facts.quote: According to most representations, the dodo had greyish or brownish plumage, with lighter primary feathers and a tuft of curly light feathers high on its rear end.

facts.statement: The dodo had a grey naked head, a beak colored green, black, and yellow, and stout yellowish legs with black claws.
facts.quote: The head was grey and naked, the beak green, black and yellow, and the legs were stout and yellowish, with black claws.

facts.statement: Subfossil remains indicate that dodos stood approximately 62.6 to 75 cm tall.
facts.quote: Subfossil remains and remnants of the birds that were brought to Europe in the 17th century show that dodos were very large birds, measuring about 62.6 - 75 cm in height.

facts.statement: A 1993 study by Bradley C. Livezey estimated male dodos weighed 21 kg and females 17 kg.
facts.quote: In 1993, Bradley C. Livezey proposed that males would have weighed 21 kg and females 17 kg.

facts.statement: A 2016 study using CT scans estimated the dodo's weight to be between 10.6 and 14.3 kg.
facts.quote: A 2016 study estimated the weight at 10.6 to 14.3 kg, based on CT scans of composite skeletons.

facts.statement: There is ongoing scientific controversy regarding the accurate weight estimates of the dodo.
facts.quote: This has also been questioned, and there is still controversy over weight estimates.

facts.statement: American geneticist Beth Shapiro and colleagues conducted the first DNA analysis of the dodo in 2002.
facts.quote: In 2002, American geneticist Beth Shapiro and colleagues analysed the DNA of the dodo for the first time.

facts.statement: The Dutch name "Walghvoghel" was first recorded in 1598 by Vice admiral Wybrand van Warwijck in his journal.
facts.quote: One of the original names for the dodo was the Dutch "Walghvoghel", first used in the journal of Dutch Vice admiral Wybrand van Warwijck, who visited Mauritius during the Second Dutch Expedition to Indonesia in 1598.

facts.statement: The origin of the name "dodo" is debated, with theories ranging from the Dutch word for "sluggard" to "Dodaars," meaning "fat-arse" or "knot-arse."
facts.quote: Some ascribe it to the Dutch word dodoor for "sluggard", but it is more probably related to Dodaars, which means either "fat-arse" or "knot-arse", referring to the knot of feathers on the hind end.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest the name "dodo" is an onomatopoeic approximation of the bird's two-note call.
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that dodo was an onomatopoeic approximation of the bird's call, a two-note pigeon-like sound resembling "doo-doo".

facts.statement: The dodo belongs to a clade of pigeons that are generally ground-dwelling and endemic to islands.
facts.quote: This clade consists of generally ground-dwelling island endemic pigeons.

facts.statement: The dodo evolved flightlessness and large size due to the lack of competing mammalian herbivores on its islands.
facts.quote: The lack of mammalian herbivores competing for resources on these islands allowed the solitaire and the dodo to attain very large sizes and flightlessness.

facts.statement: Despite adaptations for large size and flightlessness, the dodo retained many skeletal features similar to smaller flying pigeons.
facts.quote: Despite its divergent skull morphology and adaptations for larger size, many features of its skeleton remained similar to those of smaller, flying pigeons.

facts.statement: The dodo was sexually dimorphic, with males being larger and having proportionally longer beaks than females.
facts.quote: The bird was sexually dimorphic; males were larger and had proportionally longer beaks.

facts.statement: The dodo had a robust skull with a hooked bill and a short cranium relative to its jaws.
facts.quote: The skull of the dodo differed much from those of other pigeons, especially in being more robust, the bill having a hooked tip, and in having a short cranium compared to the jaws.

facts.statement: The dodo's scleral rings were formed by eleven small bones, a count similar to other pigeons.
facts.quote: The scleral rings inside the eye were formed by eleven ossicles (small bones), similar to the amount in other pigeons.

facts.statement: The dodo's sternum was large in absolute size but small relative to its body compared to flying pigeons.
facts.quote: The sternum was large, but small in relation to the body compared to those of much smaller pigeons that are able to fly.

facts.statement: The dodo had a wider pelvis than the Rodrigues solitaire and other relatives.
facts.quote: The pelvis was wider than that of the solitaire and other relatives

facts.statement: Most contemporary descriptions of the dodo come from ship logs and journals of Dutch East India Company vessels that visited Mauritius during Dutch rule.
facts.quote: Most contemporary descriptions of the dodo are found in ship's logs and journals of the Dutch East India Company vessels that docked in Mauritius when the Dutch Empire ruled the island.

facts.statement: One of the earliest accounts of the dodo is found in a journal from 1598 by van Warwijck.
facts.quote: One of the earliest accounts, from van Warwijck's 1598 journal, describes the bird as follows:

facts.statement: The sketches in the Gelderland journal are attributed to the professional artist Joris Joostensz Laerle and a second, less refined artist.
facts.quote: They have been attributed to the professional artist Joris Joostensz Laerle, who also drew other now-extinct Mauritian birds, and to a second, less refined artist.

facts.statement: The traditional image of the dodo as a very fat and clumsy bird may be exaggerated.
facts.quote: The traditional image of the dodo is of a very fat and clumsy bird, but this view may be exaggerated.

facts.statement: A famous painting by Roelant Savery from 1626, known as Edwards's Dodo, has become the standard image of the dodo.
facts.quote: A famous painting of his from 1626, now called Edwards's Dodo as it was once owned by the ornithologist George Edwards, has since become the standard image of a dodo.

facts.statement: An Indian Mughal painting rediscovered in the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg in 1955 depicts a dodo alongside native Indian birds.
facts.quote: An Indian Mughal painting rediscovered in the Hermitage Museum, St. Petersburg, in 1955 shows a dodo along with native Indian birds.

facts.statement: The dodo in the Mughal painting likely lived in the menagerie of Emperor Jahangir in Surat, India, where traveler Peter Mundy claimed to have seen two dodos between 1628 and 1633.
facts.quote: The bird depicted probably lived in the menagerie of the Mughal Emperor Jahangir, located in Surat, India, where the English traveller Peter Mundy also claimed to have seen two dodos sometime between 1628 and 1633.

facts.statement: Based on weight estimates, researchers suggest the male dodo could reach an age of 21 and the female 17.
facts.quote: Based on weight estimates, it has been suggested the male could reach the age of 21, and the female 17.

facts.statement: Studies of the dodo's leg bone strength indicate it could run quite fast.
facts.quote: Studies of the cantilever strength of its leg bones indicate that it could run quite fast.

facts.statement: Differences in historical depictions led to theories about sexual dimorphism, seasonal variation, and different species, but these are not accepted today.
facts.quote: Differences in the depictions led ornithologists such as Anthonie Cornelis Oudemans and Masauji Hachisuka to speculate about sexual dimorphism, ontogenic traits, seasonal variation, and even the existence of different species, but these theories are not accepted today.

facts.statement: It is impossible to determine if variations in beak markings, tail feathers, and coloration in accounts reflect reality, signal age or sex, or are merely inconsistent.
facts.quote: Because details such as markings of the beak, the form of the tail feathers, and colouration vary from account to account, it is impossible to determine the exact morphology of these features, whether they signal age or sex, or if they even reflect reality.

facts.statement: The dodo likely ate fallen fruits, nuts, seeds, bulbs, and roots.
facts.quote: In addition to fallen fruits, the dodo probably subsisted on nuts, seeds, bulbs, and roots.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the dodo may have also eaten crabs and shellfish.
facts.quote: It has also been suggested that the dodo might have eaten crabs and shellfish, like their relatives the crowned pigeons.

facts.statement: Contemporary sources indicate the dodo used gastroliths to aid digestion.
facts.quote: Several contemporary sources state that the dodo used gastroliths (gizzard stones) to aid digestion.

facts.statement: A 2016 study found the dodo's upper jaw was rhynchokinetic, affecting its feeding behavior.
facts.quote: In 2016, the palaeontologist Leon Claessens and colleagues found that skeletal elements of the dodo's upper jaw appear to have been rhynchokinetic (movable in relation to each other), which must have affected its feeding behaviour.

facts.statement: The dodo's beak could withstand high force loads, indicating a diet of hard food.
facts.quote: The beak also appears to have been able to withstand high force loads, which indicates a diet of hard food.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the dodo's visual abilities indicate it may have been crepuscular to avoid heat and competition.
facts.quote: The visual abilities of the dodo possibly reflect a shift towards becoming more crepuscular (active during dusk and dawn), which could help it avoid intense heat during the day and forage when there was less competition from other species.

facts.statement: The dodo's upper beak could process more tactile information than other pigeons.
facts.quote: The dodo's upper beak could also process more tactile information than other pigeons.

facts.statement: The dodo probably nested on the ground because it was flightless and had no natural enemies on Mauritius.
facts.quote: As it was flightless and terrestrial and there were no mammalian predators or other kinds of natural enemy on Mauritius, the dodo probably nested on the ground.

facts.statement: A 2017 study used bone histology and other data to recover information about the dodo's life history.
facts.quote: A 2017 study examined the histology of thin-sectioned dodo bones, modern Mauritian birds, local ecology, and contemporary accounts, to recover information about the life history of the dodo.

facts.statement: Dodo chicks grew rapidly to near-adult size and reached sexual maturity before the Austral summer or cyclone season.
facts.quote: The chicks grew rapidly, reaching robust, almost adult, sizes, and sexual maturity before Austral summer or the cyclone season.

facts.statement: The dodo is recorded as extinct by 1690.
facts.quote: extinct: 1690
